In 2016 Clément Delangue

Julien Chaumond

Thomas Wolf 

raised about a million dollars to make a business around an AI chatbot...

The now infamous Attention is All you need transformers paper Google put out, the one that powered the current AI insanity we're living through right now, hadn't dropped yet....

That came out in 2017. So in 2016, for these 3 cofounders, their AI chatbot would have been technically limited,
think about how Alexa and Siri used to feel... that's what they would have been working with technology wise.
So when Google dropped their Transformers paper in 2017, and then more importantly a year later in 2018 Google released BERT, an open weights LLM

It's worth noting a lesser known company gpt1 dropped a little bit before Bert was released... both models followed the same basic formula.

A foundational model following the "Attention is all you need" architecture, followed with two stages of learning, phase one is unsupervised, you feed it blindly all the data you can, and phase two is supervised, you slowly, using humans back then, reinforce it to behave like you want it to... like a chat bot...
No one was really paying attention to OpenAI, but Bert was getting a lot of attention... here's an example of it in action, I ask it what the capital of New Jersey is, and it correctly says Newark.
I ask it what two plus two is equal to, and it correctly says the answer is One.

So for a company working on an AI chatbot? Well suffice to say they took notice...

They wanted to adopt Bert. Tweak it.. fine tune it... you mgiht even say transform it

And so they released pytorch pretrained bert version 0.1.1

That's a mouthful...

but importantly this became the foundation of the popular transformers library that's an industry standard for working with open source models today...

This represented a transition in the company's history, from a company focused on a single chatbot, to a company focused on providing the infrastructure that powers open source models

And so a couple years later, they launched the hub... a platform that now hosts all of the most popular open source models in the world, the code required to run them, as well as a lot of open training data

I want to introduce you to The Stack. This is a dataset on HuggingFace. It has 3 terrabytes of permissive code scraped from GitHub.

I wanted to visualize how much data this is for you all... Like if I were to print it out, how many pages would this be?

I was thinking about how I could visualize this much data... Like if we were to print it out, how big would the stack be?

I started thinking, maybe I could print it out, and show you. And it turns out the cheapest way to print 550 pages is to publish a book in Amazon self publish marketplace

So that's what I did, and that's what I'm holding here... you can buy your own copy on amazon too if you want, but you can't fit the whole stack in one clean volume, so how many volumes do you need for the whole set? Well it's actually here, right on the cover...

If you're struggling to read roman numerals that large, I'll help you out. It's 14,029,886 total volumes that would be needed to print the whole stack.

If you're trying to visualize what that might look like, let me help you out
That's 288 miles stacked cover to cover, if put on a shelf, the shelf would stretch from New Jersey to Maryland.
The publishers of the Stack published a second version, a V2, the V2 is more than 10 times larger, representing 3000 miles of books on a shelf.

The stack is ONE of 883,000 datasets on HuggingFace.

And it isn't even the largest dataset, in fact it's an order of magnitude smaller than some of the larger datasets on the Hub.

I'm going to tell you some stories about this data,

but what you have to keep in mind is there is no metaphor I can give you that really wraps your mind around how much data this is. And there isn't enough time in a million conference talks to tell you all the stories contained in this data.

The first story I'm going to tell you... doesn't even occur on the hub... it strikes at the very definition of what open AI even means. Models aren't exactly source code.. so how can the source be open? is open source even the right word for an open model?
That question... almost tour an open source non-profit called the Open Source Initiative apart
Who even are the OSI? and why should you care? Well in the 90's their founder coined the term "Open Source"

And many governments for years recognize their definition of open source software...

Why does it matter how a government defines open source?
The short answer is regulation. Allow me to introduce you to the European AI act, which gives special carveouts to Open Source models, lowering their legal and compliance overhead burden
So why did this almost break the OSI? Disagreements over the definition of open-source when it comes to AI models... and at the heart of it? Data.
Should datasets, like the 880,000 datasets already hosted on huggingface, be a requirement in order to call an open source model, open source?

A question that was so charged, the OSI suspended their board election, because they didn't want a new board member with radical views on this topic... and the radical view in question? That the data should be open as part of the open-source defintion.

You can find the petition online containing hundreds of names, upset with this outcome... so why? Why resist open data as a part of open models? What is it about opening up the data that seems so impractical to the OSI board, they put themselves in this frankly embarrassing crossroads?

To answer that question... we need to zoom in on some of the data
Way way in... to one file.. in one dataset

Picture this... it's a warm day in March, you're a nutanix employee, and you have this great idea to make AI better at identifying security vulnerabilities.

Your idea is simple. If you collect a bunch of semgrep and github security issues off of github, you could feed that into an AI learning to spot vulnerabilities, and see if the AI can produce the same issues the existing github and semgrep issues flagged...

So you get ready to do this massive scrape of github... to get the github issues and run the scans, you generate a GitHub API key, a personal access token, and you kick off a massive massive scrape, and semgrep scan.
You pull it off. A huge undertaking, but the largest collection of public semgrep scans ever completed.. now free and open to the world
ANd when I say open... what I mean is apache licensed... 8.6 gigs of semgrep scans and github issues, Apache 2 licensed, free for the world to use
Except there's one small problem that you didn't notice... that little PAT that you used at the start of the story...
Well that was a classical PAT. And you gave it the repo scope...
At this point... some of you might be have put the pieces together...
Semgrep scans of their internal repos... but it gets worse
Because semgrep saves secrets it finds in cleartext... all the hardcoded secrets from these internal semgrep scans got leaked...
Let's zoom back out
Our next story started in 2023... when an anonymous developer in the AI community named comfyanonymous, started the ComfyUI project, to build with stable diffusion with more flexibility...

Imagine the power of complex image generation workflows... no longer a simple prompt, but stages, that can introduce refinement and tweaks, repeatability, with fixed seed values, maybe one stage builds a beach, the next stage puts a person on the beach, tweak the second stage without losing the first stage...

Sounds powerful, right? Compelling?

One of those early decisions was to optionally embed the workflow, prompts, everything used to create the image, so anyone could recreate it pixel accurately, and modify it themselves...

Except... the word optionally is doing some heavy lifting there... for a default behavior

And everything used to create the image?? Well... if you're not using a local open source model...

That has to include an API key doesn't it?

How many people use Comfy and doesn't know their prompts, workflows, and API keys are embedded inside their images?

I sure wouldn't have known if we weren't specifically scanning for keys in huggingface...
It's time to zoom back out
